questions.prompt: The loop transfer function \(L(s)\) is the product of
options: every block you meet walking once around the loop
the closed-loop gain and the sensitivity
the numerator and denominator of the plant
questions.explanation: Walk from the error, through the forward path, through the return path, back to the summing junction. Multiply every block you pass. That product is \(L(s)\). The reference and output are signals, not gains. The closed-loop gain times sensitivity equals \(T \cdot S = L/(1+L)^2\), which is not \(L\). The numerator and denominator of the plant describe only the forward block.

questions.prompt: The forward gain is 10 and the return gain is 0.2. The loop gain \(L\) is
questions.explanation: \(L = GH = 10 \times 0.2 = 2\). Adding the gains gives 10.2, which is not the loop product. Dividing gives 50, which is the inverse of the return gain times the forward gain.

questions.prompt: Same loop. The closed-loop gain is
questions.explanation: \(T = G/(1+L) = 10/(1+2) = 10/3 = 3.333\). The loop gain 2 is not the closed-loop gain. Adding 1 to \(G\) instead of to \(L\) gives \(10/11\), which is wrong.

questions.prompt: A unity-feedback loop has forward gain \(G = 6\). The loop gain is
questions.explanation: Unity feedback means \(H = 1\), so \(L = G \times 1 = 6\). The closed-loop gain \(6/7\) is not the loop gain. Subtracting 1 from 6 gives 5, which is not defined by the diagram.

questions.prompt: Same unity loop with \(G = 6\). The sensitivity \(S = 1/(1+L)\) is
questions.explanation: \(S = 1/(1+6) = 1/7 = 0.143\). The complementary sensitivity \(T = 6/7\) is one minus this. The loop gain 6 is not the sensitivity.

questions.prompt: The complementary sensitivity \(T(s)\) and the sensitivity \(S(s)\) satisfy
questions.explanation: \(T = L/(1+L)\) and \(S = 1/(1+L)\). Their sum is \((L+1)/(1+L) = 1\). Zero is wrong because both \(T\) and \(S\) are positive. Their product is \(L/(1+L)^2\), not 1. Their difference is \((L-1)/(1+L)\), not \(L\).

questions.prompt: Forward gain 8, return gain 0.5. The return difference \(1 + L\) is
questions.explanation: \(L = 8 \times 0.5 = 4\), so \(1 + L = 5\). The loop gain 4 is one less than the return difference. The closed-loop gain \(8/5\) is not the return difference.

questions.prompt: Same loop. A disturbance of magnitude 1 adds at the output. The fraction remaining at steady state is
questions.explanation: A disturbance at the output is divided by \(1 + L = 5\), so \(1/5 = 0.2\) remains. The closed-loop gain \(8/5\) is what a reference sees, not a disturbance. The loop gain 4 is not the rejection ratio.

questions.prompt: On a Nyquist plot, the loop gain \(L(j\omega)\) is plotted as \(\omega\) sweeps from 0 to \(\infty\). The critical point is at
questions.explanation: Stability depends on encirclements of \(-1\), the point where \(1 + L = 0\). The origin is where \(L = 0\), not the critical point. The point \(+1\) is where \(L = 1\), which is not the instability boundary. The point \(j\) is on the imaginary axis and is not special for stability.

questions.explanation: At \(s = 0\), the loop gain is \(L(0) = 12 \times 1 = 12\). The closed-loop gain \(12/13\) is what the reference sees. The sensitivity \(1/13\) is the disturbance attenuation.

questions.prompt: Robust performance requires that the loop gain satisfy constraints on
options: both magnitude and phase across frequency
questions.explanation: Robust performance bounds depend on how \(L(j\omega)\) moves in the complex plane. That requires magnitude and phase at every frequency. The DC gain alone is a single point. The forward or return alone is not the loop product.
